opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one I think about almost every day, because at an early-stage startup, every single hire changes the company.

The first thing I look for is **self-drive**. In a big company, there's structure: someone gives you a task, a deadline, a review process. In a startup, a lot of the time nobody tells you what to do next. The problems are ambiguous and the priorities shift. So I want people who see a problem and just go solve it, without waiting for permission. People who treat the company's problems as their own problems.

The second is **learning ability over current skill set**. Technology moves incredibly fast, especially now in graphics and AI. What you know today may be half obsolete in two years. So I care less about whether someone has already done exactly this job and more about how quickly they pick up new things. When I interview, I like to ask about something they taught themselves, how they approached it, where they got stuck, and how they got unstuck. That tells me a lot.

Third, **taste and a high bar**. This is harder to describe, but there are people who are satisfied once something works, and people who keep asking whether it's elegant, whether it's fast enough, whether the user will actually love it. Building Taichi taught me that the difference between a tool people tolerate and a tool people love is often in those last details. I want people who care about that.

And finally, **honesty and low ego**. Startups make lots of mistakes. What matters is how fast you notice and correct them. That only works if people can say "I was wrong" or "I think this direction is wrong" openly, without it becoming political. Someone extremely talented but unable to take feedback can actually slow the whole team down.

If I had to summarize: I want people who are driven, who learn fast, who care deeply about quality, and who are easy to work with. Credentials matter much less to me than those four things. Some of the best people I've worked with didn't have the most impressive résumés, but they had that fire.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about who I most want to bring onto the team, the first thing I look for is genuine curiosity, especially the kind that shows up as someone having built things nobody asked them to build. When I was working on Taichi during my PhD, the people who ended up contributing the most weren't necessarily the ones with the most impressive résumés. They were the ones who would see a weird performance bug and just couldn't let it go until they understood exactly what the compiler was doing. That kind of itch is very hard to teach.

The second quality is what I'd call ownership across the stack. In a small startup, there's no such thing as "that's not my job." Someone might be writing a GPU kernel in the morning and talking to a user about why their simulation crashed in the afternoon. I want people who are comfortable going from a low-level detail all the way up to asking "does this actually matter for the user?" and back down again. Engineers who only want to live in one layer struggle in that environment.

Third, and this one took me a while to appreciate, is taste. Both technical taste and product taste. Can you tell the difference between a clever solution and a good one? Can you recognize when an API is going to be painful six months from now? Taste tends to correlate with having shipped things that real people used and then having to live with the consequences. So I pay a lot of attention to whether someone has that feedback loop in their history.

And finally, I look for people who are honest about what they don't know. Startups move fast and you make a lot of decisions with incomplete information. If someone can say "I'm not sure, let me go find out" instead of bluffing, that makes the whole team faster and safer. Confidence is great, but calibrated confidence is what actually compounds.

If I had to compress all of that into one sentence, I'd say I'm looking for people who would be building something interesting on a Saturday even if nobody was paying them, and who are self-aware enough to know when they're wrong.

astra-6.text:
I look for people who are curious, who can learn quickly, and who take ownership. In a startup, you’re constantly facing problems you haven’t solved before, so having all the right experience matters less than being willing and able to figure things out.

I also value people who can turn ideas into something real. When they encounter a problem, do they wait for instructions, or do they investigate, try a solution, and ask for help when they need it? And can they work well with others—communicate clearly, take feedback, and change their minds? Those qualities make a big difference on a small team.
